summary: The first of BBN's regular reports on how available ARPANET hosts were, based on talks with sites and daily test logins from a prototype Terminal IMP. It lists hosts excluded from testing. This version had many typing errors and was reissued as RFC 240.

eli5.summary: A school-style attendance sheet for network computers, saying which ones are open for visitors. It had mistakes, so a corrected one came out.

questions: how did bbn test host availability
subtitle: Periodic reports on which ARPANET hosts were available for use.

tldr.problem: The early ARPANET needed regular updates on which hosts were available for other sites to access.
tldr.mechanism: BBN established a system of reporting host status every two weeks, based on talks with site operators and daily automated login tests from their Terminal IMP.
tldr.outcome: This RFC began a series of status reports that became standard practice, though this first version had many typing errors and was reissued as RFC 240.

facts.label: Testing frequency
facts.value: Daily, at random times on weekdays

today: RFC 235 was replaced by RFC 240 because this version contained many typing errors. The practice of regular ARPANET host status reports continued as standard operational practice.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 235 reports on the status of most ARPANET hosts for the period September 13 through September 24, 1971. BBN (Bolt, Beranek and Newman) established regular status reports to give all sites visibility into which hosts were available for network access.

The information came from two sources: direct communication with operators at each site about their plans, and daily automated testing. BBN's prototype Terminal IMP attempted to log into each accessible host at a random time each weekday.
sections.eli5: BBN called up computer centers to ask which machines were ready to talk on the network, and also tried logging in automatically each day to check.

sections.title: Host Testing Categories
sections.content:
Not all hosts were tested daily. Some hosts fell into two categories that were excluded: hosts not expected to offer services for at least a month (such as the PDP-10 at Rand, Lincoln's TX2, and machines at Stanford, Case, and Carnegie), and hosts that were user-only (Terminal IMPs at Ames, MITRE, and BBN itself, plus the Network Control Center).

This allowed BBN to focus testing on the hosts that were actually expected to be available as network servers, giving more reliable status data.
sections.eli5: Some computers weren't ready yet or were only visitors, so BBN didn't test them. The report only checked the ones that might actually serve other sites.

sections.title: Status Data
sections.content:
The RFC includes tables showing the status of each host on specific dates and times in September 1971. Status codes indicate whether a host was reachable: D for dead or unreachable, R for refused connection, T for timed out without responding, 1/2 O for half-open (connected then closed immediately), and O for open and accessible.

These daily snapshots gave the network community a clear picture of availability patterns across the ARPANET.
sections.eli5: The report used simple codes: D meant dead, R meant refused, T meant too slow, and O meant the computer was ready to talk.
